items.title: Postmodern Repo Copier Template
items.text:
Postmodern Repo Copier Template is a Copier template. Run against a destination path, it generates a repository with the hard/boring stuff already wired up.

Template Author: describe what your template does here.

items.title: What It Automates
items.text:
• Versioning and Releasing
  • Security and Dependency Updating
  • Linting, Styling, and Testing for every Commit and Pull Request
  • Publishing Documentation
  • License and Policies
  • Contribution Guide and Automatic Contributor Crediting

items.title: The Big Decision
items.text:
Make one decision before you use this template:

  • project_type (Standard or Template): whether the generated project is a repo to build in (Standard) or a child Copier template that others can build on (Template).

items.title: Inheritance
items.text: This template was built from Postmodern Repo Copier Template, and the projects and child templates it generates inherit from it the same way. copier update carries that inheritance: run against a generated project, it brings in what changed upstream (features, fixes, security patches) and keeps local customizations.

items.title: Applying to Existing Projects
items.text:
1. Complete the Prerequisites, including Secrets and Tokens.

  2. Get the existing project ready: cloned locally, with all changes committed and its default branch (usually main or master) checked out.

  3. In the existing project, create a branch from the default branch, such as copier-template-apply.

  4. Clone this repository, open it in your terminal, and install the tools the template needs:

    mise trust
mise install

  5. From this repository, run the command below, replacing the path at the end with your existing project's root:

    mise x "--" copier copy --trust https://github.com/natescherer/postmodern-repo-copiertemplate ~/path-to-existing-project

    See Template Questions for what each prompt controls.

  6. For the Repo Setup Actions question, choose Set Repo Rules on GitHub or None on Azure DevOps. Azure DevOps reads pipeline YAML from the remote repo, so register its pipelines by hand once the files are pushed; see Manual Repo Settings.

  7. Answer the other questions for your project.

  8. Review each changed file with git diff, and keep, discard, or adjust the change.

  9. Commit and push, then merge through a pull request.

The project now works the same as one generated from this template. You can delete your clone of this repository: mise run copier-update fetches the template from its URL.

items.title: Creating a New Project
items.text:
1. Complete the Prerequisites, which include installing mise.
  2. Clone this repository and open it in your terminal.

  3. Install the tools the template needs:

    mise trust
mise install

  4. Create the project, replacing the path at the end with where it should go:

    mise x "--" copier copy --trust https://github.com/natescherer/postmodern-repo-copiertemplate ~/local-repo-path-here

See Template Questions for what each prompt controls.

items.title: GitHub App Installations
items.text:
Install each of these apps for the user or organization that will own your repos. Give each one access to all repositories, so you only do this once instead of for every new repo.

  1. Renovate GitHub App
    • Opens dependency update PRs.
  2. [Optional] Codecov GitHub App
    • Connects the repo to codecov.io for coverage uploads, PR comments, and checks.
    • Skip it if you'll answer no to code_coverage.
  3. [Skip for Private Repos] AllContributors GitHub App
    • Credits contributors in the README.

items.title: Failed Workflow Alerts
items.text:
To get alerts when a workflow run fails, open Notification settings, choose how to be notified under Actions, and enable Only notify for failed workflows.

GitHub sends a scheduled workflow's notifications to whoever created the workflow or last changed its cron schedule, not to everyone with access to the repo.

items.title: One-Time Actions per Azure DevOps Project
items.text:
So that squash-merge commit titles stay valid Conventional Commits, turn off Include PR ID in the completion commit message title by default under Project settings > Repositories > Settings > All Repositories Settings.

The release, docs, and Renovate pipelines push branches and open PRs as the pipeline's build service identity. Which identity that is depends on Project settings > Pipelines > Settings > Limit job authorization scope to current project for non-release pipelines: when it's on (the default for new projects), pipelines run as <Project> Build Service (<Org>); when it's off, as Project Collection Build Service (<Org>).

Under Project settings > Repositories > Security, select that identity and set these to Allow:

  • Contribute
  • Contribute to pull requests
  • Create branch

items.title: Universal
items.text:
1. Install mise, which installs every other tool this project uses.
  2. Activate mise in your shell.

items.title: Platform-Specific
items.text:
GitHubAzure DevOps
  1. Install the GitHub CLI. Setup uses it to create the repo and apply its settings from .github/settings.yml, through gh-settings, which mise installs. Your login needs admin access to the repo.
  2. Log in to the GitHub CLI: 
    gh auth login
  3. Set up Git authentication over HTTPS, with either:
    • gh auth setup-git, so Git reuses the GitHub CLI's credentials.
    • Git Credential Manager, which also handles Azure DevOps. Git for Windows includes it; on macOS and Linux, install it separately.
  1. Install the Azure CLI.
  2. Install its Azure DevOps extension and log in: 
    az extension add --name azure-devops
az login
  3. Install Git Credential Manager to authenticate Git over HTTPS. Git for Windows includes it; on macOS and Linux, install it separately.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
1. Complete the workstation prerequisites.

  2. Clone the repo and, from its root, run:

    mise trust
mise install

mise install installs every tool this project uses at its pinned version, then installs prek's Git hooks: linters and formatters run on each commit, and committed checks each commit message. To run every hook against the whole repo:

mise x -- prek run -c .config/prek.toml --all-files

items.title: Branching
items.text:
This project uses GitHub Flow: one long-lived branch, main, plus a short-lived branch for each change.

  • main is always releasable. Everything on it has passed PR Validation, and any push to it can become the next release; see Releasing. Nothing lands on main except through a pull request; branch protection on GitHub and branch policies on Azure DevOps enforce that.
  • One change per branch, branched from the latest main. Keep it short-lived: open the pull request early, merge it once it's green, and delete the branch.
  • Branches stay independent. Branch from main, not from another unmerged branch, so pull requests can merge in any order. If main moves on, rebase onto it.
  • There are no develop, release, or hotfix branches. A fix for something already released is just another branch from main, and the release PR picks up whatever has merged since the last release.

items.title: Commits and Pull Requests
items.text:
Commit messages and PR titles follow Conventional Commits (type: summary). The type decides the next version bump; see Releasing.

PR Validation checks that the PR title is a Conventional Commit and runs the prek hooks against every file the PR changes. On GitHub, PRs are squash-merged, so the PR title becomes the commit message on main.

items.title: Tasks
items.text:
Run any of these with mise run <task>.

Task What it does copier-update Pulls in the latest parent template changes; see Updating from the Parent Template set-lifecycle Changes only the lifecycle answer, without pulling in a template update docs-server Serves these docs locally with live reload provision-secrets Sets the secrets CI needs, via masked prompts; see Secrets and Tokens renovate-lookup Runs Renovate locally in dry-run mode to show what it detects, without pushing anything; see Adding a Dependency or Tool migrate-azdo-pipeline-names (Azure DevOps only) Brings existing pipeline registrations in line after a template update renames or merges their files test Runs the render-validation test suite template-docs-server Previews the template's docs rendered under every answer combination integration-test-gh / integration-test-azdo Creates real throwaway repos from this template and checks them; see Integration Testing integration-test-verify-update-gh / integration-test-verify-update-azdo Verifies a manually updated integration-test repo integration-test-cleanup-gh / integration-test-cleanup-azdo Deletes every integration-test repo (and, on Azure DevOps, pipeline), including those of a run that stopped partway

items.title: Adding a Dependency or Tool
items.text:
Pin every dependency to an exact version, never a range, latest, or an unversioned install script, so every contributor and CI run gets the same one and Renovate can propose each bump. Where it goes depends on what it is:

  • Command-line tools (linters, formatters, build and release tools): add them to mise.toml, or mise.ci.toml if only CI needs them. A pin in a .jinja file under template/ also needs a {#- renovate: datasource=... depName=... #} comment above it, which this repo's custom managers match.
  • Libraries and packages: declare them in the language's own manifest or lockfile. Renovate detects many of these natively, but not every ecosystem or file format.

Then:

  1. Confirm Renovate detects it. Run mise run renovate-lookup and check that the dependency appears, with the right version, in the packageFiles with updates log entry. Renovate skips an unsupported manifest, and a custom manager regex that captures too much, without an error.
  2. Add a custom manager if it doesn't. A regex entry under customManagers in renovate.json can track a version Renovate can't find on its own, such as one inside a script.
  3. Group duplicates. If one dependency is pinned under two names (for example, as a mise tool and as a CI step), a packageRules entry with a shared groupName bumps both in one PR.
  4. Explain any gap. If a dependency has no trackable version source at all, say why in a comment next to where it's installed.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: Docs live in docs/ and are built with Zensical. Add every new page to nav in zensical.toml; the render-validation tests fail on a page missing from it.

items.title: Extending This Template
items.text:
This template supplies what any Git-tracked project needs, whatever it contains: repo settings, CI/CD, release automation, and repo hygiene. It's meant as a common ancestor. A Python library template, a PowerShell module template, or a Terraform template starts from a copier copy of this one with project_type: Template, which gives it its own copy of template/ to build on, and then adds what its domain needs.

What keeps this template correct has to carry over to yours. The render tests, Renovate coverage, CI on both platforms, and migrations for existing projects are all generic. This page covers applying them to what you add, starting with the decision that shapes the rest.

items.title: Start here: will other templates build on yours?
items.text:
Decide this first; it sets how much of this page applies to you. The extensible_template question records the answer.

Leaf template (most common)Extensible template

Your template produces finished projects, and nothing copies from it again. This is the lower-maintenance path, and the right default unless you know otherwise. Answer no to extensible_template, and the template handles the rest:

  • Your template/ leaves out this template's template-only files (its copier.yml, tests, scripts, and template docs), so you only maintain what your projects use.
  • The files it keeps have no is_template, is_standard, or is_extensible conditions: each update folds them out, so only the conditions that still vary remain.
  • Your copier.yml has no project-type questions or copy-template-files task; every project it creates is Standard.
  • The obligations below about your own template's extensibility don't apply.

Your template can itself be copied with project_type: Template, the relationship this repo has to yours. Answer yes to extensible_template. That costs maintenance for as long as the template exists:

  • Your copier.yml keeps project_type and extensible_template, so your projects can be templates too.
  • Your template/ keeps the whole is_template-gated subtree, to carry forward.
  • Write a guide like this page for whoever extends your template. Adapt this one: most of it (dependency pinning, Renovate coverage, the CI checklist, the testing layers) applies to any Copier template.

When a leaf template is the right call

An internal, single-company template is usually a leaf template. Nobody will fork it, and the Template/Standard branch costs its maintainers indefinitely: an extra question to explain, extra conditionals, and extra answer combinations for the render-validation suite. Choose an extensible template when you know another template will build on yours.

items.title: The mental model
items.text:
Everything in this template varies along a few axes. Every question, file, and check either applies to all combinations or is gated to the ones it belongs to:

  • developer_platform (GitHub / Azure DevOps): most capabilities exist on both platforms. A GitHub Actions workflow has an Azure Pipelines counterpart, a GitHub secret has a pipeline variable, and so on. using_github and using_azdo gate the differences.
  • project_type (Template / Standard): is_template gates what only a Copier template needs (the template/ subtree, the integration test scripts, this page), and is_standard is its complement. Whether your template keeps this axis is the decision above.
  • Your own axes. A Python library template might add a package_manager question (uv / poetry); a Terraform template might add terraform / opentofu. The render-validation suite has to exercise each answer and each combination of answers; see Testing what you add.

Each new axis multiplies the combinations everything else has to work for. When two ideas are close, add an option to an existing axis instead of a new axis.

items.title: Workflow: extending the template
items.text: Use the checklist below that matches your change. Most changes need one; a larger change, such as a new tool that also needs a secret and a CI check, works through several in turn.

items.title: Adding a new versioned dependency or tool
items.text: Follow Adding a Dependency or Tool. It covers the renovate: comments that pins under template/ need, and how to check that Renovate detects them.

items.title: Adding a new Copier question
items.text:
1. Add the question to copier.yml, with a when: or validator: if it's conditional or constrained.
  2. Use each of its values in some ANSWER_MATRIX entry in answer_matrix.py (in each copy of the suite; see Template-level tests), and add a combination each new validator: should reject to INVALID_ANSWER_MATRIX. AGENTS.md lists the rules, including _old_tag_overrides for a value the last release doesn't accept; test_answer_matrix_coverage.py catches a missed choices: value.
  3. If the question changes what a fresh copier copy sets up, update _message_after_copy and the template-questions reference in docs/ to match.

items.title: Adding a new CI workflow or pipeline
items.text:
1. Build both platform variants together; a gap left for later tends to stay. Follow the naming convention: Category (Auto/Manual): Name on GitHub, Category (Auto/Manual) - Name on Azure DevOps.
  2. Register it on Azure DevOps. Pipelines there are registered objects, not just files, so add it to the az pipelines create tasks in _tasks.
  3. Add a check to the integration test scripts: a check_*() function, and on Azure DevOps the pipeline's display name in PIPELINE_DISPLAY_NAMES in integration_test_azdo.py.
  4. Add what can't be automated to the integration test runbooks (docs/maintaining/integration-testing/runbook-github.md and runbook-azdo.md) as exact steps, such as checking a third-party bot's response.
  5. If it needs a secret, work through the next checklist too.
  6. Put any new SHA-pinned action, Azure Pipelines task version, or embedded tool version through the dependency checklist above.

items.title: Adding a new secret or credential
items.text:
1. Document its purpose and required scopes in docs/reference/token-permissions.md.
  2. Add it to the provision-secrets task (gh secret set or az pipelines variable create), so setup stays one guided step.
  3. Check for it in every workflow or pipeline that uses it: the require-secrets composite action on GitHub, or the equivalent guard step on Azure DevOps. A missing secret then fails with a clear message instead of a confusing error later.
  4. Add it to the "Before CI works" secrets list in _message_after_copy for each platform that needs it.
  5. If it can expire, consider an expiration check, for example in the monthly repo health check: authenticate as the credential, read the expiration date the platform's API reports, and notify before it lapses.

items.title: Renaming or removing something
items.text:
A rename has to reach every project that already has the old name. A plain file rename or removal needs nothing extra: copier update deletes what the template dropped and adds what it gained, like any other change.

  1. Update every reference to the old name: the integration test scripts, the manual verification checklists, and any list that enumerates things by name, such as PIPELINE_DISPLAY_NAMES. Those lists are the easiest reference to miss.
  2. If existing content has to change shape (reformatting a file so a tool can parse it, or converting old data), add a _migrations entry. Don't give it a version:: Copier checks that against the version of the template a project updates from, which in a child template's projects is the child's own version. Make it safe to rerun, a no-op once its work is done, and let it run on every update.

Live registered objects aren't files

Copier's diff only reaches files. An Azure DevOps pipeline registration exists only as a remote API object, and _tasks runs only on copier copy, so renaming a pipeline's file leaves its registration pointing at the old path. migrate_pipeline_names.py repoints the registration in place, keeping its ID, run history, and variables; see its docstring.

items.title: Testing what you add
items.text: Two things need testing separately: whether the template renders correctly, and whether what it produces works.

items.title: Template-level tests
items.text:
These test the Copier mechanics (questions, conditionals, CI/CD scaffolding), independent of your domain content, in three layers:

  • pytest tests/ runs locally and on every PR, with no external side effects. It renders every answer combination and checks for valid Jinja, YAML, and JSON, working internal links, and consistent config. New ANSWER_MATRIX entries and validator: constraints get exercised here.
  • Integration testing (integration_test_github.py and integration_test_azdo.py) creates real repos and runs real workflows and pipelines against them. It catches regressions that need a real API call, a running pipeline, or an external system. Run it before each release.
  • The integration test runbooks hold every step of a run, and their manual steps cover the rest: human judgment, and systems the scripts can't inspect, such as whether a bot responded.

A CI/CD change tested only by the first layer is untested where it's most likely to break. Verify it on a real platform.

An extensible template has two copies of the suite. PR Validation runs root tests/, and the templates built on yours inherit template/{% if is_template %}tests{% endif %}/. Add each new or changed test to both, so your CI runs it and your descendants get it. A test they shouldn't inherit goes in root tests/ only. copier update keeps the test files you add to root tests/ and merges your edits into this template's, such as answer_matrix.py. A leaf template's template/ has no tests, so its tests go in root tests/.

items.title: Tests for what the template produces
items.text:
This template is pure scaffolding with no workload of its own; yours has one. A Python library template produces Python libraries, and a Terraform template produces Terraform configs. That content needs its own checks on top of the template-level layers:

  • Starter or example code (a sample module, a sample stack) should pass its own test suite, linter, and type checker. Starter code that renders but doesn't work passes every template-level test and fails the first time a user runs it.
  • CI that tests the workload (the generated project's tests, linting, terraform validate) goes through the same Adding a new CI workflow or pipeline checklist as any other workflow.
  • The domain's own dependencies and tools (a package manager, a linter, a language server) go through the Adding a new versioned dependency or tool checklist; Renovate coverage includes them too.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: Knope computes versions, updates the changelog, and publishes GitHub Releases from Conventional Commits.

items.title: Normal Releases
items.text:
Every push to main opens or updates a release PR (branch knope/release) for the next version, computed from the commit messages since the last release:

  • fix: bumps the patch version, feat: bumps minor, and a ! or BREAKING CHANGE: commit bumps major.
  • Before 1.0.0, each shifts down one place: a breaking change bumps minor (0.1.2 to 0.2.0), and feat: and fix: both bump patch (0.2.0 to 0.2.1).
  • Renovate's chore(deps): PRs add a Dependency-Update: footer for each bump, so they bump patch too, under a Dependencies heading.
  • Changesets from template updates are included.

Merging the release PR tags and publishes the release.

A push with nothing release-worthy, such as a docs: commit or a chore: commit other than Renovate's, logs "Nothing to release yet." and leaves the release PR as it is.

Each push to main also adds a commit to the release PR, authored as github-actions[bot]. GitHub holds the PR's required check on each of those commits until someone clicks Approve and run workflow in the Actions tab, and branch protection blocks the merge until then. That's the cost of not needing a repo-wide Personal Access Token, which enterprise accounts often can't use.

items.title: Prereleases
items.text: To cut a prerelease (alpha, beta, or rc), run the "Release (Auto): Prepare Release PR" workflow from the Actions tab on GitHub, or the "Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release" pipeline from Azure Pipelines on Azure DevOps, and choose a label (on Azure DevOps, a label other than none). Each run increments that label's number (1.1.0-alpha.0, then .1). The same label can't run twice at the same commit, so push a new commit first; a different label (alpha to beta) can run at any commit.

items.title: Graduating to 1.0.0
items.text:
While the lifecycle is Pre-Alpha, Alpha, or Beta, commits only bump the minor or patch version (see Normal Releases), so Knope never reaches 1.0.0 on its own. When you're ready, run mise run set-lifecycle and choose Stable. That sets .config/knope-release-override.json to 1.0.0. Once that change is on main, the release PR proposes 1.0.0, and prereleases count up toward it (1.0.0-rc.0, 1.0.0-rc.1). Merging the release PR publishes it.

The same file pins any other version: change the version in it and merge. Knope ignores it once the released version reaches it, so it never needs removing.

items.title: Setup
items.text:
mise says the config isn't trusted. mise won't read a mise.toml it hasn't been told to trust. Run mise trust from the repo root, then mise install.

Copier stops at the Repo Setup Actions question. That question's validator checks the platform CLI before anything runs, and its message says what's missing: install gh or az, run gh auth login or az login, add the Azure DevOps extension with az extension add --name azure-devops, or (for Create Repo) put knope on your PATH. See Prerequisites. Choosing None skips the check, and the setup it guards.

Copier says the destination repository is dirty. Copier won't copy over or update uncommitted changes. Commit or stash them, then run it again.

items.title: Releases
items.text:
No release PR opens. In order of likelihood:

  • Nothing since the last release bumps the version: docs: commits don't, and neither do chore: commits other than Renovate's. That's expected; see Releasing.
  • On GitHub, Actions isn't allowed to open pull requests. Enable Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests; see Manual Repo Settings.
  • On Azure DevOps, the build service identity can't push branches or open pull requests. Grant it the repository permissions in Prerequisites.

The release PR can't merge because its check never runs. On GitHub, each push a bot makes to the release PR waits for someone to click Approve and run workflow; see Releasing.

items.title: Dependencies
items.text: Renovate doesn't update a dependency. Run mise run renovate-lookup and check whether the dependency appears, with the right version, in the packageFiles with updates log entry. If it doesn't, Renovate can't see it; see Adding a Dependency or Tool. If it does, on GitHub check that the Renovate app has access to this repo.

items.title: Template updates
items.text: copier update fails while rendering your project's old version. See Updating from the Parent Template.

items.title: Updating from the Parent Template
items.text:
This project was generated from the Postmodern Repo Copier Template Copier template. On the 1st of each month, the Monthly Maintenance workflow/pipeline's Copier Update Check job checks for a new template release and sends a notification to APPRISE_URL when one is available; see Secrets and Tokens.

To pull in its latest changes:

  1. Start from a clean working tree on a new branch; Copier won't update over uncommitted changes.
  2. If the update crosses a major version, read that release's Breaking Changes in the template's changelog first; see its Stability Policy.
  3. Run mise run copier-update. It reuses your recorded answers and asks only the questions added since your last update.
  4. Resolve any conflicts where your own edits overlap a template change; Copier marks them inline.
  5. Review the new files in .changeset/, one per relevant upstream change, and delete the ones that don't apply to your project. Each links to the upstream PR it came from.
  6. Commit and open a pull request as usual. The remaining changesets go into your next release with your own commits.
  7. On Azure DevOps, if the update renamed, merged, or removed files under .azurepipelines/, run mise run migrate-azdo-pipeline-names once the pull request has merged to main. It repoints an existing registration at each new name, keeping its run history and variables, and deletes the registrations of pipelines merged into another. Wait for the merge: Azure DevOps reads pipeline YAML from main, so repointing earlier breaks every run until the new files get there. It's safe to run when nothing needs migrating.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
If copier update fails while rendering your project's old template version (for example, because that version depends on something that no longer exists), re-apply the current template over the project:

  1. Copy .config/copier-answers.yml to a temporary file outside the repo and delete every key that starts with _ from the copy.

  2. Run:

    mise x -- copier copy --trust --overwrite --data-file <temporary-answers-file> https://github.com/natescherer/postmodern-repo-copiertemplate .

  3. Unlike copier update, this overwrites your own edits. Review every changed file with git diff, and restore what you'd customized before committing.

items.title: Upgrading from 0.x
items.text: 1.0.0 is this template's first stable release; from here on, it follows the Stability Policy. How a 0.x project gets there depends on the version it was last updated to, recorded as _commit in its Copier answers file.

items.title: From v0.7.14 or later
items.text:
Update as Updating from the Parent Template describes, but in place of mise run copier-update, run this once from your project's root:

mise x -- uvx --refresh --from copier@latest --with jinja2-shell-extension copier update --answers-file .config/copier-answers.yml --skip-answered --trust

A 0.x project's copier-update task runs the Copier its mise.toml pins, which is older than this release's _min_copier_version. The command above is what the task runs from this release on: the newest Copier and jinja2-shell-extension. Copier's migrations seed .config/knope-current-version.json from your latest release tag and reformat your changelog for Knope. An update that spans many releases writes many changesets to .changeset/; delete the ones that don't matter to your project's users, or replace them with one summary changeset. Then work through After either path.

items.title: From before v0.7.14
items.text:
Copier renders your project's old version alongside the new one to work out what changed. Releases before v0.7.14 need Jinja extensions current tooling doesn't install, and some of their questions have since been renamed, so update once with a command that supplies both:

  1. Start from a clean working tree on a new branch.

  2. If the answers file is .copier-answers.yml at the repo root (before v0.4.0), move it to .config/copier-answers.yml and commit that on its own.

  3. Template projects only: Copier doesn't manage template/, so remove the files the parent deleted from it since your version yourself. From your project's root (in Git Bash on Windows), with your answers file's _commit as <old-version> and the release you're updating to as <new-version>:

    git clone --branch <new-version> https://github.com/natescherer/postmodern-repo-copiertemplate ~/template-clone
git -C ~/template-clone diff --name-only --no-renames --diff-filter=D <old-version> <new-version> -- template | xargs -I{} git rm -q --ignore-unmatch "{}"
git commit -m "chore: remove files the parent template deleted"

  4. From your project's root, run the update. If your answers file has project_short_description, add -d project_description="<same text>"; if it has license: Provide Own, add -d license=None.

    mise x uv -- uvx --refresh --from copier@latest --with copier-templates-extensions --with copier-template-extensions --with jinja2-time --with jinja2-shell-extension --with githubkit --with requests --with python-slugify --with packaging copier update --trust --skip-tasks --skip-answered --answers-file .config/copier-answers.yml --vcs-ref <new-version> -d repo_setup_actions=None

    --skip-tasks keeps your old version's setup tasks from rerunning; they'd try to create the repo again from your recorded answers. Copier's migrations still run, so the version file and changelog headings are handled the same way as on the other path.

  5. Template projects only: copy the parent's current template/ into yours (in Git Bash on Windows), which the skipped tasks would otherwise have done:

    cp -r ~/template-clone/template/. template/

  6. Resolve conflicts and review .changeset/ as for any update, then work through After either path.

items.title: After either path
items.text:
On GitHub:

  • Close the old release PR. A project from before v0.8.0 released with release-please; close any open release-please PR and delete its branch. Knope opens its own.
  • Delete REPO_MAINTENANCE_PAT. Workflows now run under the default GITHUB_TOKEN. The update prints a reminder if the secret is still set; delete it under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions, and revoke the token if nothing else uses it.
  • Approve bot-authored workflow runs. Without the token, someone has to click Approve and run workflow before checks run on each push a bot makes to a PR, such as the release PR; see Releasing.
  • Switch from the Settings GitHub App to gh-settings. gh-settings now applies .github/settings.yml, in its own format, which the update writes. Once the update has merged to main, remove this repo from the Settings app's repository access (or uninstall the app), so it stops reading the file, then run mise run sync-repo-settings. It shows what it will change and asks first; this also applies the Actions and GitHub Pages settings settings.yml now covers.
  • Check the repo settings. Code scanning and private vulnerability reporting, which a fresh copy enables when it creates a public repo, aren't applied by an update; see Manual Repo Settings.

On Azure DevOps:

  • Repoint renamed and merged pipelines. v0.8.0 renamed the files under .azurepipelines/, and 1.0.0 merges the Copier Update Check, Renovate, and Repo Health Check pipelines into Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance, merges Create Prerelease into the release pipeline, and renames the docs pipeline to Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit, as on GitHub. Once the update has merged to main, run mise run migrate-azdo-pipeline-names. It repoints the Renovate registration (or another of the three) at Monthly Maintenance, keeping its variables, deletes the other merged registrations, and repoints any v0.8.0-renamed one. Azure DevOps reads pipeline YAML from main, so running it before the merge breaks every pipeline run until the new files get there. Monthly Maintenance needs APPRISE_URL and GITHUB_COM_TOKEN; add whichever its registration lacks (see Secrets and Tokens).
  • Add GITHUB_COM_TOKEN. The Renovate pipeline now requires it, since Renovate skips every dependency hosted on github.com without one, and the other pipelines use it to keep mise's downloads under github.com's rate limit; mise run provision-secrets sets it on all of them. See Secrets and Tokens.
  • Register new pipelines. A pipeline added since your version that no old one was merged into isn't registered by an update or by migrate-azdo-pipeline-names, which warns about it. Register each .yml directly in .azurepipelines/ that isn't yet, and delete any registration whose file no longer exists; see Manual Repo Settings.

Everywhere:

  • Set new secrets. Run mise run provision-secrets; see Secrets and Tokens.
  • Review .changeset/ before you merge, as above.
  • Move edits from moved docs pages. The generated docs/ now uses getting-started/, maintaining/, and reference/ folders. If you'd edited a page that moved (such as a Standard project's docs/releasing.md, now docs/maintaining/releasing.md), carry your changes over, and update any links to the old paths.
  • Move CLAUDE.md content into AGENTS.md. CLAUDE.md is no longer generated, since Claude Code reads AGENTS.md directly. If you'd added your own content to it, move that into AGENTS.md.

items.title: Integration Testing
items.text: Integration testing is the last check before every release. It creates real repos from the current template source and exercises them on GitHub and Azure DevOps, which catches the regressions a local render can't: repo creation, pipeline registration, and workflow runs. The template ships for both platforms, so a release is tested on both, whichever platform this repo uses.

items.title: Repo A and Repo B
items.text:
Each run creates two repos per platform, named <prefix>-integration-test-<timestamp>-a and ...-b, with different answers, so one run covers more of the answer space.

  • Repo A is a copy at HEAD. The script runs every automated check against it: it dispatches pipelines, opens PRs, and cuts a release and a prerelease.
  • Repo B is a copy at the last stable release tag, left at that tag for a person to update. Running the update the way a real user does, prompts included, shows each new question as users will see it. A second entry point to the script then checks that the update applied cleanly.

The two repos also split each either/or answer: code_coverage is on for Repo A and off for Repo B on both platforms, and on GitHub, zensical_target is GitHub Pages for Repo A and docs-site Directory in Repo for Repo B.

items.title: Automated and Manual Checks
items.text:
The scripts automate every check they can: they dispatch pipelines and wait for them, open PRs and confirm they're blocked or pass, push commits and confirm the release flow responds, and cut a release and a prerelease. A failure doesn't stop the run, so one run reports everything.

Two setup steps keep the checks independent of timing. Repo A first merges a setup PR that pins an old dependency and lifts Renovate's schedule for it alone, so Renovate has one PR to open on any day; commits a minimal coverage.xml, so PR Validation's coverage step has a report to publish; and has its link check skip this template's published docs, whose new pages exist only once this release publishes them. Repo B merges a setup PR with the same link check skip, since the update brings in links to those pages. At the newest release, it records the commit just before that release on a branch, so the update check finds a newer release there without rendering any other version.

The terminal shows only an outline of a run: each step and each check's [PASS] or [FAIL], with timestamps, a spinner under the step in progress, and a summary at the end. Everything else goes to the run's log under .cache/integration-test/, for analysis after the fact: every command and its output, timestamped, and the log of every workflow or pipeline run it waited on.

The runbooks' manual steps cover the rest, as fixed steps that are the same on every run: anything that needs human judgment (whether a badge renders, whether each setup checklist item applies) and anything the scripts can't read (a pipeline step's log on Azure DevOps, or whether the Renovate and All Contributors apps responded on GitHub).

The scripts find test repos by name, so their cleanup also removes what a run that stopped partway left behind. Each repo's local clone is named after it too, so cleanup deletes those, and keeps the temp directory from filling up with old runs. On Azure DevOps, deleting a repo leaves its pipelines registered, so the cleanup deletes those as well.

items.title: How It Differs from pytest tests/
items.text: pytest tests/ (mise run test, and CI on every PR) checks the template locally: it renders into a temporary directory, never contacts GitHub or Azure DevOps, and runs no repo setup tasks. It catches broken Jinja, invalid YAML and JSON, dead links, and update-path bugs, including a real copier update against a git history (test_update_from_last_tag). Integration testing covers what needs a real API call, a running pipeline, or an external system.

items.title: Runbooks
items.text:
Each platform's runbook holds every step of a run, from setup to cleanup:

  • Integration Test Runbook (GitHub)
  • Integration Test Runbook (Azure DevOps)

items.title: Integration Test Runbook (Azure DevOps)
items.text:
Every step of an Azure DevOps integration test run, from setup to cleanup, as the last step before a release. See Integration Testing for what the run does and why.

The steps use these values from each repo's entry in the run's summary: Repo A's Name for <repo-a>, and each repo's Local clone for <repo-a-path> and <repo-b-path>. Each entry's Web link opens that repo in Azure DevOps. <template-repo-path> is this template's own clone, and <org> and <project> are the Azure DevOps organization and project the test repos go in.

Checkbox state isn't saved

You can tick the boxes as you go, but reloading or leaving the page clears them. Finish the list in one sitting.

items.title: Before You Start
items.text:
• The Azure DevOps Prerequisites are in place for <project>: the project settings, the build service permissions, and the Azure CLI with its Azure DevOps extension, logged in.
  • A GitHub token is available: log in with gh auth login, or set the GITHUB_COM_TOKEN environment variable to a GitHub token with no scopes. The run sets it on every pipeline, for mise's tool downloads and Renovate's lookups on github.com, and stops before creating anything without one.

  • <org> and <project> are set for the integration-test tasks, once per machine, in <template-repo-path>/mise.local.toml, which git ignores:

    [env]
INTEGRATION_TEST_AZDO_ORG = "<org>"
INTEGRATION_TEST_AZDO_PROJECT = "<project>"

    A template hosted on Azure DevOps defaults to its own org and project, so it needs this only to test somewhere else. Passing --org and --project to a task overrides either.

items.title: Running the Test
items.text:
• Start the run:

    cd <template-repo-path>
mise run integration-test-azdo

  • When it finishes, its summary says "all checks passed" for both repos. If a check failed, find out why in the run's log directory, which the run prints at its start and end: <template-repo-path>/.cache/integration-test/<timestamp>-azdo/. Its run.log holds everything the run printed and every command's output, and each pipeline run the script waited on has its own log beside it. Fix the cause, clean up (see Cleaning Up), and start again.

items.title: Repo A
items.text: A copy at HEAD, with code_coverage on.

items.title: After First Setup
items.text:
Automated: a bad PR title fails PR Validation, the branch policy blocks completing it, and Project Administrators can bypass the policy.

  • Each item in the setup checklist (repeated under Repo A in the run's summary) applies to an Azure DevOps project, and each link in it opens.
  • The badges at the top of README.md render, with no broken images.
  • README.md shows docs/assets/images/readme-logo.png and docs/assets/images/readme-screenshot.png.

items.title: Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance
items.text:
Automated: the run starts each of the pipeline's three jobs alone, through its Job to run parameter, and each succeeds. The Copier Update Check job completes; what it reports isn't checked, since az can't easily read a run's step output (see the script's module docstring). The Repo Health Check job completes clean. The Renovate job, with Repo A's Renovate schedule lifted, typos pinned to an old release, and your GitHub token set as GITHUB_COM_TOKEN, opens a PR bumping typos.

  • The Copier Update Check job's Check for Template Updates step reports no update available, since this repo is at HEAD.

  • Push a branch with a broken link:

    cd <repo-a-path>
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c integration-test/broken-link
echo "[Broken link](https://httpbin.org/status/404)" >> README.md
git commit -am "docs: add a broken link"
git push -u origin integration-test/broken-link

  • In <project>'s Pipelines, run [<repo-a>] Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance on that branch (Run pipeline, then Branch/tag: integration-test/broken-link and Job to run: repo_health_check). The run fails, and its log names https://httpbin.org/status/404.

items.title: Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit
items.text:
• Merge a docs change through a PR:

    cd <repo-a-path>
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c integration-test/docs-change
echo "Integration test docs change." >> docs/index.md
git commit -am "docs: integration test docs change"
git push -u origin integration-test/docs-change
az repos pr create --source-branch integration-test/docs-change --target-branch main --title "docs: integration test docs change" --merge-commit-message "docs: integration test docs change" --auto-complete true --squash true --delete-source-branch true

  • Once that PR completes, [<repo-a>] Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit runs, opens a PR from zensical-build, and completes it. docs-site/index.html on main then contains "Integration test docs change."

items.title: Test (Auto) - PR Validation
items.text:
Automated: a bad PR title fails, and a failing test suite fails and blocks completing the PR.

  • The PR Validation run for the docs-change PR has a Code Coverage tab showing the results of the coverage.xml that Repo A's setup PR commits.

  • Open a PR from the broken-link branch, then push one more commit to it:

    cd <repo-a-path>
git switch integration-test/broken-link
az repos pr create --source-branch integration-test/broken-link --target-branch main --title "docs: add a broken link"
git commit --allow-empty -m "docs: push again"
git push

    The PR shows a second PR Validation run, started by the push. Azure Repos has no PR trigger, so only the build validation policy starts this pipeline.

items.title: Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release
items.text:
Automated: a docs-only commit releases nothing, a feat: commit opens a release PR with the bumped version in its title, and merging that PR creates a tag.

  • Repo A has exactly one tag without a prerelease suffix (-alpha or -beta): the release from the feat: merge. The run merged fix: integration test prerelease commit right after that release, and the pipeline tells that merge apart from the release PR's own through an API check, not a native trigger, so it mustn't have published again.

items.title: Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release: Prereleases
items.text:
Automated: a manual run with each prerelease label produces a matching tag, the same label at the same commit is blocked, and a different label at the same commit is allowed.

Nothing left to check for Repo A.

items.title: Repo B
items.text: A copy at the last stable release tag, with code_coverage off. It stays at that tag until you update it.

items.title: Before Updating
items.text:
Automated, before you update anything: Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance's Copier Update Check job runs and completes, on main and on the integration-test/older-recorded-version branch, whose answers record the commit just before the newest release.

  • The main run's Check for Template Updates step reports no update available, since Repo B is at the newest release.
  • The branch run's Check for Template Updates step reports the newest release and sends the notification without an error.

items.title: Running the Update
items.text:
• Update on a branch to this template's HEAD, the release candidate, pressing Enter at each prompt to accept the default:

    cd <repo-b-path>
git switch -C integration-test/copier-update
mise x -- uvx --refresh --from copier@latest --with jinja2-shell-extension copier update --answers-file .config/copier-answers.yml --skip-answered --trust --vcs-ref=HEAD

    This is the upgrade guide's command, not Repo B's copier-update task: Repo B starts at a 0.x release, whose task runs a Copier older than this template's _min_copier_version.

  • The update finishes without an error. Then commit it and open its PR:

    git add -A
git commit -m "chore: copier update"
git push -u origin integration-test/copier-update
az repos pr create --source-branch integration-test/copier-update --target-branch main --title "chore: copier update" --merge-commit-message "chore: copier update" --auto-complete true --squash true --delete-source-branch true

    Without --merge-commit-message, Azure DevOps squash-merges with a generic "Merge pull request N" message instead of the PR title.

items.title: After Updating
items.text:
• Once the update's PR completes, repoint or delete any pipeline registrations it renamed or merged:

    cd <repo-b-path>
git switch main
git pull
mise run migrate-azdo-pipeline-names

  • Verify the update:

    cd <template-repo-path>
mise run integration-test-verify-update-azdo

    It finds the newest run's Repo B, with its org and project, from its local clone. It checks that the update brought in current content, left no conflict markers, registered each pipeline only under its current name, removed the merged pipelines' old registrations, and that Test (Auto) - PR Validation triggers and passes on a new PR. Every check prints [PASS].

items.title: Cleaning Up
items.text:
• Delete the test repos and their pipelines, and confirm when it asks:

    cd <template-repo-path>
mise run integration-test-cleanup-azdo

    It deletes every integration-test repo and pipeline in the project, and their local clones, including any left by a run that stopped partway.

items.text:
Every step of a GitHub integration test run, from setup to cleanup, as the last step before a release. See Integration Testing for what the run does and why.

git switch -C integration-test/copier-update
mise x -- uvx --refresh --from copier@latest --with jinja2-shell-extension copier update --answers-file .config/copier-answers.yml --skip-answered --trust --vcs-ref=HEAD

    cd <repo-b-path>
git switch main
git pull
mise run sync-repo-settings

mise run integration-test-verify-update-gh

mise run integration-test-cleanup-gh

items.title: Azure DevOps Limitations
items.text:
Azure DevOps support is deprecated and will be removed in a future major version. It stays for organizations that require it; use GitHub for new projects unless you need Azure DevOps.

Azure DevOps support is best-effort, and differs from GitHub in these ways:

  • No public projects. Azure DevOps projects are assumed to exist for organizational requirements.
  • No GitHub-only features, such as custom issue labels.
  • Partial branch protection. Repo setup creates a required build validation policy on the default branch (Test (Auto) - PR Validation must pass before a PR completes), plus a Project Administrators bypass permission that matches GitHub's admin bypass. Unlike GitHub's ruleset, it doesn't block force pushes or deleting the default branch. With repo_setup_actions: None, set it up by hand with Manual Repo Settings.
  • zensical_target is always docs-site Directory in Repo. GitHub Pages isn't offered, so there's no release-versioned docs site; see Features.
  • Renovate runs as a pipeline job, not an app. The Renovate job in .azurepipelines/maint-auto-monthlymaintenance.yml runs on a schedule and authenticates with the pipeline's own $(System.AccessToken), not a stored secret. It pushes branches and opens PRs as the build service identity, so it needs the same permissions as the release and docs pipelines; see Prerequisites.
  • The release pipeline detects PR merges through the API. The release flow matches GitHub's: every push to main opens or updates the knope/release PR, and merging it publishes the release; see Releasing. Azure Pipelines has no "PR completed" trigger, only push triggers, so Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release checks whether the last completed PR from knope/release into main matches the commit that started the run. A prerelease is a manual run of the same pipeline (Pipelines, select it, Run) with a prerelease label instead of none.
  • No semantic linter for pipeline YAML. ryl checks .azurepipelines/*.yml as YAML, but no standalone tool checks Azure Pipelines schemas the way actionlint checks GitHub Actions workflows.

items.title: Workstations
items.text: Windows, macOS, and Linux are all supported. mise run tasks and Git hooks work from any shell mise is activated in, including PowerShell, Bash, and zsh.

items.title: Tools
items.text:
mise installs every tool this project uses, at the version pinned in mise.toml. Two minimums apply on top of that, and Renovate keeps both current:

  • mise itself must be at least the min_version in mise.toml. An older mise refuses to run and says so; mise self-update fixes it.
  • Copier must be at least the parent template's _min_copier_version. mise run copier-update runs the newest Copier, so this only matters if you run Copier some other way, which also needs Python 3.11 or later for the template's migrations.

items.title: CI
items.text: GitHub Actions workflows and Azure Pipelines both run on hosted ubuntu-latest runners. A self-hosted runner needs Linux with Bash, Git, and curl, plus PowerShell 7 and jq on Azure DevOps; mise installs everything else.

items.title: Support for Multiple CI/CD Platforms
items.text:
• GitHub Recommended
    • Creating repos under both users and orgs is supported
  • Azure DevOps Deprecated
    • See Azure DevOps Limitations for the features it lacks and why it's being phased out

items.title: Support for Public (Open-Source) and Private (Closed-Source) Repositories
items.text: Both public (open-source) and private (closed-source) repos are supported. See project_visibility for what differs.

items.title: Support for Existing Projects
items.text: The template can create a new project or apply to an existing repo. See Applying to an Existing Project.

items.title: Support for Template Updates
items.text: Copier keeps projects in sync with their parent template. A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow/Azure DevOps pipeline checks for new template releases, and mise run copier-update applies them. See Updating from the Parent Template.

items.title: Support for Child/Recursive Templates
items.text: Build your own template from this one; it can keep receiving this template's updates. See Template Projects and Extending This Template.

items.title: Project Lifecycle
items.text: A project's lifecycle (Pre-Alpha, Alpha, Beta, Stable, or Inactive) drives a managed notice at the top of the README. Lifecycle only moves forward (Pre-Alpha to Alpha to Beta to Stable); Inactive is reachable from any state. Change it with mise run set-lifecycle.

items.title: AI Agent Instructions
items.text: Optionally (via agent_instructions), an AGENTS.md describes the project's conventions for AI coding agents.

items.title: Code Coverage Reporting
items.text: Optionally (via code_coverage), PR validation publishes a Cobertura coverage.xml from the repo root to Codecov on GitHub, or to Azure Pipelines' built-in coverage reporting on Azure DevOps. Your own test command produces the file.

items.title: Repository Management
items.text:
• Creation of new repos and branches
  • Repo settings and branch protection (on GitHub, applied from .github/settings.yml by gh-settings); see Manual Repo Settings
  • On Azure DevOps, a build validation policy requiring PR Validation to pass before a PR completes, with a Project Administrator override
  • Creation of useful non-default issue labels: awaiting pr and blocked
  • On public GitHub repos, CodeQL code scanning and private vulnerability reporting are enabled
  • Contributor management and crediting via All Contributors
  • Dependency updates via Renovate; the GitHub Marketplace App on GitHub, a self-hosted scheduled pipeline on Azure DevOps
  • mise run renovate-lookup, a local Renovate dry run that shows which dependencies it detects before you push
  • A monthly repo health check that link-checks the whole repo
  • On GitHub, each scheduled workflow re-enables itself on each scheduled run, so GitHub doesn't disable it after 60 days without repo activity
  • Notifications via Apprise (Slack, Teams, email, and many more) when a template update is available, plus on Azure DevOps when Renovate opens PRs and when a docs PR merges or needs attention; mise run provision-secrets sets the secrets these need (see Secrets and Tokens)

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
Documentation is set up with Zensical, the successor to the end-of-life mkdocs-material.

  • Multiple choices of documentation target:
    • GitHub Pages: built and versioned for each release, keeping earlier versions
    • A docs-site folder in the repo: rendered HTML for offline use, rebuilt from the latest main
  • Local preview via mise run docs-server
  • Starter pages for prerequisites, releasing, updating from the parent template, secrets, and manual repo settings

items.title: Code Management and Formatting
items.text:
• Repo-local dev tool installation via mise, with tool caches kept under .cache/; see Development
  • Linting and formatting on every commit via prek:
    • Commit message linting via committed
    • GitHub Actions linting via actionlint
    • .github/settings.yml validation via gh-settings (GitHub only); PR Validation also reminds you to apply a changed file after merging
    • Link checking via lychee
    • Markdown linting via rumdl
    • Python linting and formatting via Ruff (Template projects only)
    • Shell script linting via ShellCheck
    • Spell checking via typos
    • TOML linting and formatting via Tombi
    • YAML linting via ryl
    • General hygiene: merge conflict markers, trailing whitespace, final newlines, byte order marks, LF line endings, and filename case conflicts

items.title: CI/CD
items.text:
• PR validation: the PR title must be a Conventional Commit, and prek runs against every file the PR changes
  • Version number calculation, changelog updating, releasing, and tagging via Knope: each push to main updates a release PR, and merging it publishes the release; see Releasing
  • A manually triggered prerelease (alpha, beta, or rc) workflow/pipeline
  • On GitHub, third-party actions are pinned to commit SHAs, and Renovate keeps those pins current

items.title: Support Files
items.text:
• .gitignore, set to ignore macOS .DS_Store files, Windows Thumbs.db files, and tool caches (plus Python bytecode caches in Template projects)
  • CHANGELOG.md, maintained by Knope
  • AGENTS.md, instructions for AI coding agents
  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, derived from The Contributor Covenant (public projects only)
  • CONTRIBUTING.md, a guide for first-time contributors (public projects only)
  • Issue forms for bug reports, feature requests, and questions, plus a chooser link for private vulnerability reports (public projects only)
  • A pull request template reminding contributors that PR titles must be Conventional Commits (public projects only)
  • LICENSE, a copy of the MIT License (public projects only)
  • README.md, laid out for a product (Standard projects) or a template (Template projects)
  • SECURITY.md, pointing vulnerability reports to GitHub's private reporting (public projects only)

items.title: Template Projects
items.text:
Choosing project_type: Template adds tooling for building and maintaining a template of your own (see Development for the full task list):

  • An unrendered copy of the parent template's template/ directory, so your template starts from (and can keep receiving) everything above. A leaf template (extensible_template: No) gets it without the template-only files or the project-type conditions in the rest, since its projects are never templates
  • A pytest render-validation suite that renders every answer combination in an answer matrix and checks the output (mise run test)
  • Integration tests that create real throwaway repos on GitHub or Azure DevOps (mise run integration-test-gh / mise run integration-test-azdo)
  • mise run template-docs-server, a live preview of your template's docs rendered under every answer combination
  • Python linting and formatting via Ruff for the template's own scripts and tests
  • On every copier update, any parent template change worth releasing is turned into a Knope changeset, so it reaches your own changelog and version bump instead of disappearing into a single update commit

items.title: Editor Configuration
items.text: Visual Studio Code settings and extension recommendations are included.

items.title: Manual Repo Settings
items.text:
GitHubAzure DevOps

gh-settings applies the settings below, from the description through GitHub Pages, from the committed .github/settings.yml: repo setup runs it when the project is copied, and mise run sync-repo-settings reapplies the file after a change. A PR that changes the file gets it validated, and a PR Validation warning reminds you to run the task after merging. It uses your gh auth login credential, which needs admin access to the repo. Without that access, have an admin run it, or apply the settings by hand in the GitHub UI as described here. .github/settings.yml holds the exact values; where this page and the file differ, the file is right.

With repo_setup_actions: None, or to reapply settings later, set up in the Azure DevOps UI what Create Repo would otherwise configure.

items.title: Description and Homepage
items.text: On the repo's main page, edit About (the gear icon) and set the description to your project_description answer. For a public repo publishing docs to GitHub Pages, also set the website to the docs site (https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/).

items.title: Labels
items.text:
Under the repo's Issues tab, open Labels, and create these alongside GitHub's defaults:

Name Color Description awaiting pr #668F04 Awaiting completion of a PR from a contributor blocked #F28C28 Blocked by an external dependency

items.title: Merge Options
items.text:
Under Settings > General > Pull Requests:

  • Disable Allow merge commits and Allow rebase merging, leaving only Allow squash merging: a squashed PR's title becomes its commit on main, which the Conventional Commits checks and release automation read
  • Enable Allow auto-merge
  • Enable Automatically delete head branches

items.title: Actions
items.text: Under Settings > Actions > General, enable Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests, and leave Workflow permissions at Read repository contents and packages permissions.

items.title: Branch Protection
items.text:
Under Settings > Rules > Rulesets, create a new ruleset:

  • Name: default-branch-protection
  • Enforcement status: Active
  • Target branches: Default branch
  • Rules:
    • Restrict deletions
    • Block force pushes
    • Require a pull request before merging, with:
      • Required approvals: 0
      • Dismiss stale pull request approvals when new commits are pushed: off
      • Require review from Code Owners: off
      • Require approval of the most recent reviewable push: off
      • Require conversation resolution before merging: off
    • Require status checks to pass, with:
      • Require branches to be up to date before merging: on
      • Status check: tests (the job in Test (Auto): PR Validation)
  • Bypass list: add Repository admin, with bypass mode Pull requests only, so repo admins can use the "Merge without waiting for requirements to be met" button.

items.title: Security and Analysis
items.text:
(Public repos only; private repos need a paid GitHub Advanced Security license.)

Under Settings > Code security, enable Secret scanning and Push protection.

items.title: GitHub Pages
items.text:
(Only if zensical_target is GitHub Pages.)

Set Settings > Pages > Source to GitHub Actions. Then, under Settings > Environments, open (or create) github-pages and set Deployment branches and tags to No restriction, since release docs deploy from a tag.

items.title: Settings Repo Setup Applies
items.text: gh-settings can't manage these, so .github/settings.yml doesn't cover them, and with repo_setup_actions: None the copy doesn't apply them. If the repo is public, enable CodeQL's default setup and private vulnerability reporting under Settings > Advanced Security.

items.title: Pipelines
items.text:
Push the generated files to main first, since Azure DevOps reads each pipeline's YAML from the repo. Then, under Pipelines > New pipeline (Azure Repos Git, this repo, Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file), create each pipeline below with exactly this name, replacing <repo> with your repo's name. Other automation, such as mise run provision-secrets, finds pipelines by name:

Name YAML file [<repo>] Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance .azurepipelines/maint-auto-monthlymaintenance.yml [<repo>] Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit .azurepipelines/docs-auto-zensicalcommit.yml [<repo>] Test (Auto) - PR Validation .azurepipelines/test-auto-prvalidation.yml [<repo>] Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release .azurepipelines/release-auto-release.yml

.azurepipelines/templates/ holds steps the pipelines share, not pipelines; don't register its files.

Or, with the Azure CLI and its azure-devops extension installed and logged in, run this for each row:

az pipelines create --name "<name>" --repository <repo> --repository-type tfsgit \
  --branch main --yml-path <yaml file> --skip-first-run true \
  --org https://dev.azure.com/<org>/ --project "<project>"

Then run Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit and Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release once each, to build the docs and open the first release PR, and set the pipeline variables listed in Secrets and Tokens.

items.title: PR-Validation Branch Policy
items.text:
Under Project Settings > Repositories > (this repo) > Policies > Branch Policies > main, add a Build Validation policy:

  • Build pipeline: the Test (Auto) - PR Validation pipeline created above
  • Trigger: Automatic
  • Policy requirement: Required
  • Build expiration: Immediately

items.title: Bypass Permission
items.text: Under Project Settings > Repositories > (this repo) > Security, select Project Administrators and set Bypass policies when completing pull requests to Allow, so project admins can use the bypass option on the Complete button.

items.title: Stability Policy
items.text: This template follows Semantic Versioning. Its public interface is everything a project generated from it depends on: the questions and what their answers do, the files it generates and where they live, and the URLs of these docs.

items.title: What counts as breaking
items.text:
A release is a major version when a project already generated from the template needs manual action after copier update to keep working the way it did. That includes:

  • Removing or renaming a question, or changing what an existing answer does.
  • Moving, renaming, or removing a generated file that projects commonly reference or customize, such as a workflow or pipeline file, or a CI job whose name a branch protection rule or required check points at.
  • Removing a supported option, such as a developer_platform.
  • Moving or removing a page in these docs, since generated projects' docs link into them.

A change that a _migrations step in copier.yml handles completely, with nothing left for the project to do, isn't breaking.

items.title: Minor and patch releases
items.text:
• Minor (feat:): new questions with a default, new generated files, new features, and newly deprecated options.
  • Patch: bug fixes (fix:), dependency bumps, and changes that leave a correctly working project's output unchanged.

Docs-only changes don't trigger a release on their own; see Releasing.

items.title: Deprecations
items.text:
Something slated for removal is deprecated first, in a minor release: the question's help text, these docs, and the changelog say so. It keeps working for the rest of that major version and is removed in the next one.

Azure DevOps support is deprecated (see developer_platform). It stays supported for every 1.x release and is removed in 2.0.0.

items.title: Updating across a major version
items.text:
copier update moves to the latest release, including across a major version. Before an update that crosses one, read that release's Breaking Changes in the changelog and follow its steps as part of the same update.

To stay on the current major for now, pass the newest tag in that major explicitly:

mise run copier-update --vcs-ref=<tag>

items.title: Template Questions
items.text:
This page covers what each Copier question controls and what it sets up. The questions not listed (repo_name, author_name, project_name, project_description) only set their own value. Repo setup authenticates through your gh auth login or az login session, not a token; see Prerequisites and Secrets and Tokens.

Questions marked as fixed after the first copy aren't asked again on update; Copier keeps the recorded answer.

items.title: developer_platform: GitHub / Azure DevOps
items.text:
Decides which platform's files are generated: .github/workflows/ for GitHub, or .azurepipelines/ for Azure DevOps. It also limits other answers: Azure DevOps projects can't use GitHub Pages for zensical_target, and project_visibility defaults to Private. See Azure DevOps Limitations. Fixed after the first copy.

Azure DevOps support is deprecated and will be removed in a future major version. Use GitHub for new projects unless you need Azure DevOps.

items.title: repo_setup_actions: Create Repo / Set Repo Rules / None
items.text:
Controls which setup runs after the copy. Choosing anything but None runs a check that the platform CLI (gh or az) is installed and logged in before Copier continues; see Prerequisites. Fixed after the first copy.

  • Create Repo creates the remote repo. On GitHub, it also sets Actions workflow permissions, sets up GitHub Pages when used, and, for public repos, enables CodeQL default setup and private vulnerability reporting. On Azure DevOps, it also registers a pipeline for each .yml file directly in .azurepipelines/.
  • Set Repo Rules (GitHub only) applies the same settings to an existing repo without creating one. Azure DevOps registers pipelines from YAML on the remote repo, which an existing project hasn't pushed at copy time, so choose None there and follow Manual Repo Settings.
  • None skips all of it; create the repo and apply its settings yourself.

GitHub projects get .github/settings.yml whatever you choose. Create Repo and Set Repo Rules apply it with gh-settings; with None, run mise run sync-repo-settings once the repo exists, or apply it by hand with Manual Repo Settings.

items.title: Repo location: github_username / github_org / azdo_org / azdo_project
items.text:
Where the repo lives. Copier asks only the pair for your developer_platform. Fixed after the first copy.

  • github_username: your GitHub username. It defaults to the username in a GitHub noreply user.email (12345+username@users.noreply.github.com); with any other email, check the default before accepting it.
  • github_org: the organization that owns the repo. Leave it as None to create the repo under github_username.
  • azdo_org / azdo_project: the Azure DevOps organization and project the repo is created in. The project name can contain spaces.

items.title: project_type: Standard / Template
items.text:
The other foundational decision, with developer_platform; see the home page. Fixed after the first copy.

Standard generates a project repo, a starting point for whatever the project is for. Template also generates:

  • its own copier.yml, so the project can be used as a Copier template, as this repo is;
  • fuller docs about the template's own features, including this page;
  • template-authoring tasks such as mise run integration-test-gh and integration-test-azdo.

See Extending This Template for what comes next: whether your template will be extended in turn, and checklists for adding to it.

items.title: extensible_template: Yes / No
items.text:
Asked only for Template: whether other Copier templates will be built from this one.

  • No (the default for a new copy) makes a leaf template. Its projects are always Standard, so its copy of template/ leaves out the template-only files (the child copier.yml, tests, scripts, and template docs) and has the is_template, is_standard, and is_extensible conditions folded out of the files it keeps. Its own copier.yml doesn't ask project_type. Most templates, such as a company's internal deployment template, are leaf templates.
  • Yes makes an extensible template. It keeps the whole template/, so its projects can be templates too, as this template's are.

An existing Template project is asked once on its next update, with yes preselected, which keeps its current behavior. Answering no then removes the template-only files from its template/. See Extending This Template.

items.title: project_visibility: Public / Private
items.text:
A Public repo is an open-source project: visible to anyone and open to contributions. A Private repo is closed-source and requires authentication to access. Fixed after the first copy. Private repos omit what only public code needs:

  • All Contributors: .all-contributorsrc and its workflow, which credit contributors in the README.
  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and CONTRIBUTING.md. Add your own if you want them; template updates leave files the template doesn't generate alone.
  • LICENSE: see license below.
  • GitHub security scanning: CodeQL default setup, private vulnerability reporting, and secret scanning with push protection. These are free on public repos and need a paid GitHub Advanced Security license on private ones; see Manual Repo Settings to enable secret scanning by hand.

items.title: license: MIT / None
items.text: Controls whether a LICENSE file is generated and whether the README states MIT licensing. It defaults to MIT for public repos and None for private ones, which can't choose MIT: a license only matters once others can see the code. With None on a public repo, the setup checklist reminds you to add a license; without one, nobody may legally use, copy, or contribute to the code.

items.title: zensical_target: GitHub Pages / docs-site Directory in Repo
items.text:
Chooses where the built docs go. Fixed after the first copy.

  • GitHub Pages: .github/workflows/docs-auto-zensical.yml deploys them, using mike to keep versions (latest, dev, and one per release).
  • docs-site Directory in Repo: .github/workflows/docs-auto-zensicalcommit.yml (GitHub) or .azurepipelines/docs-auto-zensicalcommit.yml (Azure DevOps) builds them into a committed docs-site/ folder, rebuilt from the latest main, with no version history. Azure DevOps projects can only use this option.

items.title: lifecycle: Pre-Alpha / Alpha / Beta / Stable / Inactive
items.text:
Controls the status notice at the top of the README. Change it with mise run set-lifecycle, which updates or removes the notice:

  • Pre-Alpha / Alpha: not ready for public use.
  • Beta: use with caution.
  • Stable: production-ready; no notice.
  • Inactive: no longer under active development.

Moving to Stable for the first time pins the next release to 1.0.0 in .config/knope-release-override.json; see Releasing.

items.title: agent_instructions: Yes / No
items.text: Whether to generate AGENTS.md, the repo's conventions for AI coding agents.

items.title: code_coverage: Yes / No
items.text: Whether to publish code coverage: through the Codecov GitHub Action on GitHub, or Azure Pipelines' built-in coverage publishing on Azure DevOps. It publishes a Cobertura coverage.xml from the repo root but doesn't generate one. Your test command, or a language-specific child template, produces it: for example pytest-cov's --cov-report=xml for Python, or Pester's -CodeCoverage for PowerShell.

items.title: Secrets and Tokens
items.text: This page lists the credentials this project needs and why. No workflow or pipeline needs a Personal Access Token: CI runs as each platform's built-in identity (GITHUB_TOKEN / $(System.AccessToken)), and repo setup uses your own CLI session.

items.title: CLI Session
items.text:
GitHubAzure DevOps

Repo setup (and, in Template projects, the integration test scripts) runs as whoever is logged in via gh auth login. That session needs the repo and workflow scopes, which gh auth login grants by default. Check with gh auth status.

Repo setup (and, in Template projects, the integration test scripts) runs as whoever is logged in via az login. That account needs access to the target Azure DevOps project, plus permission to create repos, pipelines, and branch policies in it.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: Once you have each value below, run mise run provision-secrets. It prompts for each one through the platform's CLI (gh secret set / az pipelines variable create), masked as you type and never passed as a command-line argument. Rerun it any time, for example to rotate a value.

items.title: APPRISE_URL
items.text: The Copier update check on both platforms needs a secret or variable named APPRISE_URL. On Azure DevOps, that check is a job in the Monthly Maintenance pipeline, whose Renovate job also notifies when it opens PRs; the docs pipeline needs it too, since it merges its own PR and notifies when that succeeds or PR validation fails. It's an Apprise URL for wherever the notifications should go: email, Slack, Discord, ntfy, Pushover, or one of 80+ other services. Apprise's docs give each service's URL format.

items.title: GITHUB_COM_TOKEN
items.text:
(Azure DevOps only.) Renovate looks up most dependency versions on github.com, and skips every dependency hosted there without a token, so Monthly Maintenance's Renovate job fails without one. Every pipeline uses it when it's set: mise downloads tools from github.com, and the Repo Health Check job checks github.com links, and Microsoft-hosted agents share github.com's unauthenticated rate limit by IP, so a run without a token can fail on a 403. Create a personal access token with no scopes on any GitHub account, then add it to each pipeline (mise run provision-secrets does this, asking for the value once per pipeline):

az pipelines variable create --name GITHUB_COM_TOKEN --pipeline-name "[<repo>] <pipeline>" --secret true

Run that for each of the four pipelines: Maint (Auto) - Monthly Maintenance, Docs (Auto) - Zensical Build & Commit, Release (Auto) - Prepare & Publish Release, and Test (Auto) - PR Validation.

items.title: CODECOV_TOKEN
items.text: (GitHub with code_coverage only.) The PR validation workflow uploads coverage.xml to Codecov with this token. Copy it from the repo's settings page on codecov.io after installing the Codecov GitHub App (see Prerequisites).
